scene: Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: Can we do this one?
Child: (both place hands on their heads, looking at the tablet)
Child: (sitting with one hand on their head, the other pointing)
Parent: Hands on my head.
Child: (places one hand on their head while one hand is pointed forward)
Child: (places both hands on their head)
Parent: Hands on the knees.
Child: (keeps both hands on their head)
Child: (still keeping both hands on their head)
Parent: Hands on someone else's knees.
Child: (smiling, but still keeps hands on their head while parent puts hands on the child's knees)
Child: (places one hand on parent's shoulder, smiling)
Parent: Hands on someone else's head.
Child: (smiling, placing both hands on their head, facing the parent)
Child: (smiling and leaning back)
Parent: Don't take off the camera 'cause it's supposed to look at you. Oh, don't play with it.
Child: (smiling, facing the parent)
Child: (looking at something off-screen, possibly the tablet)
Parent: Are they curious? Wait, are they looking at that one, that one, that one, that one, that one, or that one?
Child: (gesturing or pointing, showing interest)
Child: (touching or scratching back of head, looking at the parent)
Parent: I don't know. [crosstalk 00:00:29] Maybe all of them.
Child: (nodding or agreeing)
Child: (still touching back of neck, looking at the parent)
Parent: When can we choose it?
Child: When they say ready.
Parent: (looking at the child, possibly nodding)
Child: (pointing to the tablet)
Parent: You can start anytime you want to now.
Child: (looking at the tablet and touching the screen)
Parent: Oh, we can start, okay, let's go.
Child: (waiting and looking at the screen)
Parent: Loading.
Child: (sitting quietly, looking at the screen while listening)

Parent: Once upon a time, there was a little house way out in the country. She was a pretty little house, and she was strong and well built. The man who built her so well said, “This little house shall never be sold, for gold or silver, and she will live to see our great-great-grandchildren's, great-great-grandchildren living in her.”
Child: (still looking at the screen, listening attentively)
Parent: The little house was very happy as she sat on the hill, and watched the countryside around her. She watched the sunrise in the morning, and she watched the sunset in the evening.
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen)
Child: (looking at the screen and following along)
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: Like one for each hour. Day followed day...
Child: (nodding and listening)
Child: (pointing at the tablet screen)
Child: (engaged and counting along)
Child: (continuing to point at the screen)
Parent: Oh, that's more than a day.
Child: (looking intently at the screen)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah. Day followed day, each one a little different from the one before, but the little house stayed just the same."
Child: (looks up at the parent)
Parent: "In the night, she watched the moon grow from a thin new moon to a full moon, then back again to a thin old moon."
Child: (nods and continues to look at the tablet)
Child: (pointing at the tablet, looking at it)
Child: (looking at the parent)

Parent: "And when there was no moon, she watched the stars. Way off in the distance, she could see the lights of the city. The little house was curious about the city and wondered what it would be like to live there. Time passed quickly for the little house as she watched the countryside slowly change with the seasons. In the spring, when the days grew longer, and the sun warmer, she waited for the first robin to return from the south. She watched the grass turn green, she watched the buds on the trees swell, and the apple tree burst into blossom. She watched the children playing in the brook."
Child: (looking at the parent)
Parent: (looking at the child, reading from the tablet)
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking at the tablet)

Parent: "In the long summer days, she sat in the sun, and watched the trees cover themselves with leaves, and the white daisy's cover the hill. She watched the gardens grow, and she watched the apples turn red and ripen, and she watched children swimming in the pool. In the fall, when the days grew shorter, the nights colder, she watched the first frost turn the leaves to bright yellow, and orange, and red. She watched the harvest gathered and the apples picked. She watched the children going back to school. In the winter, when the nights were long, and the days were short, and the countryside covered with snow, she watched the children coasting, and skating."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, appears to be engaged)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand close to mouth, showing curiosity)

Parent: "Year followed year, the apple trees grew old, and new ones were planted. The children grew up and went away to the city, and now at night, the lights of the city seem brighter and closer. One day, the little house was so surprised to see a horseless carriage coming down the winding country road. Do you know what a horseless carriage is?"
Child: (thinking, continues to look at the tablet, appears to be pondering the question)
Child: (sitting next to the parent, looking somewhat disinterested, hand near face)
Parent: "No."
Child: (appears to be listening but not actively engaged)
Parent: (pointing at the tablet) "What do you think we drive in? Car? There are no horses. Anyway, pretty soon, there were more of them on the road and fewer carriages pulled by horses."
Child: (still appears somewhat disengaged, hand near face)

Parent: (continuing to read from the tablet) "Pretty soon, along came some surveyors and surveyed a line in front of the little house. Pretty soon, along came a steam shovel, and dug a road through the hill covered with daisy's. Then some trucks came and dumped big stones on the road. Then some trucks with little stones. Then some trucks with tar, and sand. And finally a steam roller came, and rolled it all smooth, and the road was done."
Child: (listening but not actively responding, hand remains near face)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand near mouth)
Parent: (pointing to the tablet screen) "Now the little house watched the trucks and automobiles going back and forth to the city..."
Child: (still looking at the tablet, focused on the story)
Child: (leaning in closer to the tablet, hand now resting on the table)
Parent: (continuing to point to the screen) "...Now it was not so quiet and peaceful at night..."
Child: (remains engaged, closely following the story)
Child: (looking at the tablet with the parent, slightly smiling)
Parent: Yeah.
Child: (still looking at the tablet, hands on lap, appears engaged)
Parent: 1, 2, 3!
Child: (looks at parent, then back at the tablet)
Parent: Oh my goodness, that's a lot of trains.
Child: (points at the tablet)
Parent: That's a elevators.
Child: (Looking at the tablet, sitting close to the parent)
Parent: Yes.
Child: (Points at the tablet, smiling)
Parent: One, I like that.
Child: (Still looking at the tablet, stops pointing)
Parent: Yeah.
Child: (Continues looking at the tablet, attentive)
Parent: I think...I think it's very efficient.
Child: (Nods, engaged in the story)
Parent: I really like that. I think she should stay, because that's like cool.
Child: (Sits back a bit, seems to think)
Parent: I think it's cool too, but some people don't like city, so, and trains.
Child: (Still looking at the tablet, listening carefully)

Parent: People were moving faster and faster. No one noticed that little house anymore, they hurried by without a glance. Pretty soon, they tore down the apartment houses and tenement houses around the little house, and started digging big cellars, one on each side. The steam shovels, dug down 3 stories on one side, and 4 stories on the other side. Pretty soon, they started building up. They built up 25 stories on one side, and 35 stories on the other. Now the little house only saw the sun at noon, and didn't see the moon or stars at night at all, because the lights of the city were too bright. She didn't like living in the city. At night, she used to dream of the country, and the fields of daisy's, and the apple trees dancing in the moonlight.
Child: (looking at the tablet, seems engaged with the story)

Parent: "The little house was very sad and lonely. Her paint was cracked and dirty. Her windows were broken, and her shutters were hung crookedly. She looked shabby, though she was just as good a house as ever underneath. Then one fine morning in spring, along came the great..."
Child: (still focused on the tablet, listening attentively)
Child: (looking slightly to the side, appearing thoughtful or curious)
Parent: "Where's the one under."
Child: (raises hand to mouth, looks like he is thinking or about to respond)
Child: (looking at the tablet, hand near mouth)

Parent: (gestures towards the tablet) "There she is... [crosstalk 00:08:48] Oh, the other trains? I don't know, maybe, oh it's because it's underground, you can't see it unless they show you. And they're just showing you what's above ground."
Child: (continues to look at the tablet)
Parent: "Oh."
Child: (still looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Along came the great-great-granddaughter of the man who built the little house so well. She saw the shabby little house, but she didn't hurry by. There was something about the little house that made her stop and look again. She said to her husband, “That little house looks just like the little house my grandmother lived in when she was a little girl. Only, that little house, was way out in the country on a hill covered with daisies, and apple trees growing around.”
Child: (listening, keeps hand near mouth)

Parent: “They found out it was the same, very same house, so they went to the movers to see if the little house could be moved. The movers looked at the little house all over, and said, “Sure! This house is as good as ever! She's built so well, we could move her anyway... anywhere.”
Child: (continues to listen attentively)
Parent: "So they jacked up the little house that she..."
Child: "This picture looks, looks all the same." (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "Yeah, well, sometimes it's the same one twice in a row."
Child: (listening and nodding)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)

Parent: "Traffic was held up for hours, as they slowly moved her out of the city. I'm sure people trying to get to work loved that. At first, the little house was frightened, but after she got used to it, she really liked it. They rolled along the big road, and they rolled along the little roads, until they were way out in the country. When the little house saw the green grass, and heard the birds singing, she didn't feel sad anymore. They went along, and along..."
Child: (listening intently)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)
Parent: "The last one was spring. Did she notice spring now?"
Child: (nodding)
Child: (pointing at the tablet)

Parent: "But they couldn't seem to find the right place. They tried the little house here, and they tried her there, they finally saw a little hill in the middle of a field, and apple trees growing around. “There!”, said the great-great-granddaughter..."
Child: (listening and smiling)
Child: (looking at the tablet)
Parent: Is it summer or spring?
Child: I don't know, what do you think?
Parent: Spring!
Child: I think spring too. That's just the place.
Parent: I think it's almost summer.
Child: Maybe.
Parent: But not yet.
Child: Like your birthday.
Parent: Mm-hmm (affirmative).
Child: Maybe.

Parent: “Yes it is!”, said the little house to herself. A cellar was dug on top of the hill, and slowly they moved the house from the road to the hill. The windows, and shutters were fixed, and once again, they painted her a lovely shade of pink. As the little house settled down on her new foundation, she smiled happily. Once again, she could watch the sun, and moon, and stars. Once again she could watch spring, and summer, and fall, and winter, come and go. Once again she was lived in, and taken care of.
Child: (looking at the tablet)

Parent: Never again would she be curious about the city. Never again would she want to live there. The stars twinkled above her, a new moon was coming up. It was spring, and all was quiet and peaceful in the country. The end.
Child: (still looking at the tablet)
Parent: Bookshelf, there you go. Okay, you want another one?
Child: (nods and points at the tablet)
Parent: The Lorax? Okay.
Child: (continues looking at the tablet)
Parent: At the far end of town, where the grickle grass grows, and the wind smells slow and sour when it blows, and no birds ever sing excepting old crows, is the street of the lifted Lorax.
Child: (lying down with their head on the parent's lap, looking somewhat drowsy, not looking at the tablet)

Parent: "Something to sleep, the grickle grass some people say, if you look deep enough, you can still see today. Where the Lorax once stood, just as long as it could, before somebody lifted the Lorax away. What was the Lorax? And why was it there? And why was it lifted and taken somewhere? From the far end of town, where the grickle grass grows, the old Once-ler still lives here. Ask him, he knows."
Child: (remains lying down, still not looking at the tablet)

Parent: (continues reading) "You won't see the Once-ler, don't knock at his door, he stays in his lerkim, on top of his store. He lurks in his lerkim, cold under the roof, where he makes his own clothes out of miff-muffered moof. And on special nights in August, he peeks out of shutters, and sometimes he speaks, and tell how the Lorax was lifted away. He'll tell you perhaps, if you're willing to pay."
Child: (still lying down, seems relaxed and not looking at the tablet)

Parent: (continues reading) "On the end of a rope, he lets down a tin pail, and you have to toss in 15 cents, and a nail, and the shell of a great-great-great-grandfather snail. Then he pulls up the pail, and makes a most careful count, to see if you've paid him the proper amount. Then he hides what you paid him, away in his snuvv, his secret strange hole, in his gruvvulouse glove."
Child: (remains in the same position, eyes open but not looking at the tablet)

Parent: (continues reading) "Then he grunts, “I will call you by whisper-ma-phone, for the secrets I tell you are for your ears alone." Slupp Down slupps the whisper-ma-phone to your ear, and the old Once-ler's whispers are not very clear, since they have to come down through a snergelly hose, and he sounds as if he had smallish bees up his nose. “Now I'll tell you,” he says with his teeth sounding gray, "how the Lorax got lifted and taken away. It all started back such a long, long time back. Way back in the days when the grass was still green, and the pond was still wet, and the clouds were still clean, and the song of the swomee-swans rang out in space. One morning I came to this glorious place, and I first saw the trees, the truffula trees. The bright-colored tufts of the truffula trees. Miles after mile in the fresh morning breeze."
Child: (still lying down, calm and seemingly comfortable on the parent's lap)
Child: (lying down across the parent's lap, head resting on the parent's leg, eyes partially closed)

Parent: "And under the trees, I saw brown bar-ba-loots frisking about in their bar-ba-loot suits, and they played in the shade, and ate truffula fruits. From the rippulous pond came the comfortable sound of the humming-fish humming while splashing around. But those trees, those trees, those truffula trees. All my life I've been searching for trees such as these. The touch of their tufts was much softer than silk, and they had the sweet smell of fresh butterfly milk. I felt a great leaping of joy in my heart, I knew just what I'd do, I unloaded my cart."
Child: (still lying in the same position, showing slight movements)

Parent: "In no time at all, I had built a small shop. Then I chopped down a truffula tree with one chop, and with great skillful skill, and with great speedy speed, I took the soft tuft, I knitted a thneed."
Child: (remains lying across the parent's lap, appearing relaxed but somewhat drowsy)

Parent: "The instant I'd finished, I'd heard a ga-zump, I looked. I saw something pop out of the stump, of the tree I'd chopped down. It was sort of a man. Describe him? That's hard, I don't know if I can. He was shortish, and oldish, and brownish, and mossy, and he spoke with a voice that was sharpish and bossy."
Child: (resting head on parent's lap, listening to the story)

Parent: "“Mister!,” he said, with a saw dusty sneeze, “I am the Lorax, I speak for the trees! I speak for the trees, for the trees have no tongues, and I'm asking you sir at the top of my lungs!” He was very upset as he shouted, and puffed. “What's that thing you've made out of my truffula tuft?”"
Child: (resting head on parent's lap, listening quietly)

Parent: "“Look Lorax,” I said, “there's no card for alarm, I just chopped one tree, I'm doing no harm. I'm being quite useful. This thing is a thneed! A thneed's a fine something that all people need. It's a shirt, it's a sock, it's a glove, it's a hat, but it has other uses, yes, far beyond that. You can use it for carpets, for pillows, for sheets, or curtains, or covers for bicycle seats.”"
Child: (still resting head on parent's lap, listening intently)
Parent: "The Lorax said, “ Sir, you are crazy with greed. There's no one on earth who would buy that fool thneed!”"
Child: (resting on parent's lap, eyes focused on the tablet)

Parent: "But the very next minute, I proved he was wrong. For just at that minute, a chap came along, and he thought that the thneed I had knitted was great, and he happily bought if for $3.98. I laughed at the Lorax, “You poor stupid guy, you never can tell what some people will buy.”"
Child: (resting head on parent's lap)
Parent: "“I repeat!” Said the Lorax, “I speak for the trees,”"
Child: (resting head on parent's lap, eyes still focused)
Parent: "“I'm busy!” I told him, “Shut up, if you please.”"
Child: (resting head on parent's lap, listening)

Parent: "I rushed across the room, and at no time at all, built a radio phone. I put in a quick call. I called on my brothers, and uncles, and aunts, and I said, “listen here, here's a wonderful chance for the whole Once-ler family to get mighty rich. Get over here fast, take the road to North Nitch, turn left at Weehawken, sharp right at South Stitch.”"
